steps: Check for a common factor first: always take out the HCF
For x² + bx + c: find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b
For difference of two squares: use a² − b² = (a+b)(a−b)
Check your answer by expanding back
method_card.title: How to Factorise Algebraic Expressions
method_card.content:
Factorising is the reverse of expanding: write an expression as a product of factors.

Common factor: take the highest common factor of every term outside a bracket. \(6x + 15 = 3(2x + 5)\).

Quadratic \(x^2 + bx + c\): two numbers that multiply to \(c\) and add to \(b\). \(x^2 + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)\).

Difference of two squares: \(a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)\), so \(x^2 - 25 = (x + 5)(x - 5)\). Always factorise fully.
method_card.example:
Factorise \(x^2 - 3x - 10\)

Step 1: Find two numbers that multiply to \(-10\) and add to \(-3\)

Step 2: \(-5 \times 2 = -10\) and \(-5 + 2 = -3\) ✔

Answer: \((x - 5)(x + 2)\)

misconceptions.message: (2x−5)² gives 4x²−20x+25, which has an extra −20x term. A difference of two squares needs one plus and one minus bracket: (2x+5)(2x−5).

misconceptions.message: (2x+25)(2x−1) mixes up the square roots. √(4x²)=2x and √25=5, so it is (2x+5)(2x−5).
misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor

gold.hint: Difference of two squares: square-root each term to get 2x and 5.

misconceptions.message: (x+5)² gives +10x in the middle, but the expression has −10x. The number is −5: (x−5)².
misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor

misconceptions.message: (x−5)(x+5) is x²−25 with no middle term. The −10x here means it is the perfect square (x−5)².
misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor

gold.hint: This is a perfect square: the number is −5, so it is (x − 5) squared.

misconceptions.message: 3(x²−4) is only half done. x²−4 is a difference of two squares, so factorise again: 3(x+2)(x−2).
misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor

misconceptions.message: (3x+6)(x−2) still hides a common factor of 3 inside the first bracket. Take it fully outside: 3(x+2)(x−2).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor

gold.hint: Take out 3 first, then factorise the difference of two squares.

misconceptions.message: (x−3)(x−3−y) expands wrongly. Group x²−6x+9 as (x−3)², then apply the difference of two squares with y: (x−3+y)(x−3−y).

gold.hint: Group x²−6x+9 as a perfect square, then use the difference of two squares with y.

misconceptions.message: 2x(x²−9) stops too early. x²−9 is a difference of two squares: 2x(x+3)(x−3).
misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor

misconceptions.message: x(2x²−18) misses part of the common factor. The HCF is 2x, and 2x²−18 factorises further: 2x(x+3)(x−3).
misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor

gold.hint: Take out 2x first, then factorise the difference of two squares.

misconceptions.message: 9(x+1) expands to 9x+9, not 3x+9. The highest common factor of 3x and 9 is 3: 3(x+3).

misconceptions.message: 3(x+9) expands to 3x+27. After dividing, 9÷3=3, so the bracket is (x+3).

misconceptions.message: 2(4x−6) is not fully factorised: 4x−6 still shares a factor of 2. The full HCF is 4: 4(2x−3).

misconceptions.message: (x+2)(x+3) gives +5x in the middle. We need −5x, so both numbers are negative: (x−2)(x−3).

problem_bank.bronze_description: Common factor: find the highest common factor of every term and take it outside a single bracket.
problem_bank.silver_description: Quadratic trinomials x² + bx + c: find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b, giving two brackets.
problem_bank.gold_description: Harder factorising: difference of two squares, perfect squares, and taking out a common factor first. Factorise fully.

steps.label: Find factor pair
steps.content: Two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5: 2 and 3

opener.label: Before any algebra
opener.display: 3 equal rows. Each row has 2 blue and 5 gold counters.

steps.say: Count one row on its own: 2 blue counters and 5 gold counters.
steps.hint: Add the two blue and five gold.

steps.say: So 21 is 3 lots of (2 + 5), which is 3 × (2 + 5). Splitting a total into equal groups is factorising: you write the shared 3 outside a bracket. Now swap the counts for \(x\): 6 blue and 15 gold become \(6x + 15\), and the same 3 rows give \(6x + 15 = 3(2x + 5)\). Taking out the common factor is exactly sharing into equal rows.
Look for the highest common factor of 6x and 15.
steps.pre: Biggest number that divides both 6 and 15:

steps.say: So \(6x + 15 = 3(2x + 5)\). Check by putting x = 1 into both forms.
steps.hint: Work out the bracket first, then times 3.

steps.say: For \(x^2 + bx + c\), find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.
steps.hint: The last number in the expression.
The number in front of x.
Work out each bracket at x = 1, then multiply.

steps.say: Two square terms with a minus between them: this is a difference of two squares. Square-root each term.

steps.hint: Work out each bracket at x = 1, then multiply.

bronze.title: Bronze: common factor
steps: Factorising reverses expanding. For a single bracket, find the highest common factor (HCF) of every term and write it outside.
Divide each term by the HCF to get what goes inside: \(6x + 15 = 3(2x + 5)\) because \(6x ÷ 3 = 2x\) and \(15 ÷ 3 = 5\).
Take out letters too. If every term has an \(x\), the HCF includes \(x\): \(5x^2 + 15x = 5x(x + 3)\). Check by expanding back.

silver.title: Silver: quadratic trinomials
steps: For \(x^2 + bx + c\), find two numbers that multiply to \(c\) and add to \(b\). They become the numbers in the two brackets.
Watch the signs. If \(c\) is positive, both numbers share \(b\)'s sign; if \(c\) is negative, one is positive and one is negative.
Write \((x + p)(x + q)\) with your two numbers, then expand to check the middle term.

gold.title: Gold: DOTS, squares and factor first
steps: Difference of two squares: \(a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)\). Square-root each term: \(4x^2 - 25 = (2x + 5)(2x - 5)\).
Always take out a common factor first, then keep going: \(3x^2 - 12 = 3(x^2 - 4) = 3(x + 2)(x - 2)\).
A perfect square has a middle term: \(x^2 - 10x + 25 = (x - 5)^2\). Check the number doubled gives the middle term.
